Subject: RFI: zonal tenancy attestations & lateral containment choreography

Vanessa —

Thanks for taking this on. As part of our procurement we need a short, evidence-backed packet addressing how Redwood implements: 1) zonal/availability boundary tenancy (how tenants are scoped to AZs or subnets), 2) controls that prevent lateral movement between tenants (both control plane and data plane), and 3) egress enforcement and proof of allowlisting (we require examples).

Could you provide:
- A labeled network diagram showing tenancy demarcation and sidecar alignment (PNG or PDF)
- A concise threat model summary (3–5 high-likelihood attack paths and mitigations)
- Examples of egress allowlist evidence (sample logs or CSV, sanitized)
- A short note on fallback behaviour (canary/fail-open policies and circuit breakers)

If you can attach the diagram and a short playbook we can review internally. Would appreciate a quick walkthrough — are you available Thu 09/23 10:00–11:00 PT?

Appreciate it — this will feed directly into our Security Review board next week.

--

Trevor / Alicia —

Thanks for the clear ask. See attached: zonal-tenancy-diagram-v2.png (high-level topology), egress-allowlist-sample.csv (sanitized), and a short containment-playbook.pdf. Below is a concise summary; Ben (cc'd) will follow up with technical depth and an inline ASCII reference topology for reviewers.

Summary (high level) — Redwood Inference:
- Zonal tenancy: Tenants are assigned to logical deployment groups which map to AZ-level subnets. Each tenant's inference pods run in tenant-scoped node pools; control-plane roles are isolated in a separate management VPC with hardened peering.
- Lateral containment: Data-plane isolation is enforced by per-tenant sidecar filters, strict network policies, and namespaces with least privilege. Control-plane interactions use mutual-TLS and role-bound service accounts to prevent cross-tenant API operations.
- Egress allowlist: Outbound flows must pass egress policy enforcement (sidecar + eBPF hooks) and are logged. Attached CSV shows sample allowlist hits with timestamps and SHA256 request IDs for correlation.
- Fallback/choreography: We support canary rollouts and circuit breakers per-route. Default is fail-closed for data-leakage paths and fail-over to a lower-capacity model variant for availability SLOs.

We can do Thu 09/23 10:00 PT for the walkthrough — Ben and I will present. If that works I'll send a calendar invite and a short agenda.

Thanks,

Trevor — quick technical addendum and an inline topology snapshot for reviewers. I'm pasting a minimal ASCII sketch of the tenant demarcation and then a short threat-model bite.

[inline topology]
Management VPC (control-plane)
  |-- Private peering -- Tenant VPCs (per-customer) -- Public Egress NAT (managed egress nodes)
  |-- HSM/KMS (opaque key service)

Tenant VPC 
  |- Tenant node-pool A (AZ-1) -> inference-pods w/ tenant-sidecar (L4+L7 filters)
  |- Tenant node-pool B (AZ-2) -> inference-pods w/ tenant-sidecar
  |- Per-tenant Redis/KV (encrypted) w/ IAM policies bound to tenant SA

Key controls (high level):
- Sidecar enforcement: Each inference pod runs a tenant-scoped sidecar implementing egress allowlist, prefix caching isolation, and token masking. Sidecars perform TLS origination for approved flows and drop unknown destinations.
- eBPF egress hooks: We run eBPF programs on host nodes to ensure kernel-level enforcement of outbound allowlists; this provides defense-in-depth beyond userland sidecars.
- Control-plane RBAC: All control-plane requests require mTLS and are authorized by a policy engine (OPA+XACML bindings). No tenant SA can modify another tenant's node pool or KV resources.
- KV segregation: Per-tenant KV namespaces with crypto-wrapped keys; requests are validated against request provenance headers that carry the per-request ID (SHA256) referenced in logs.
- Circuit breakers & canary: We enforce token-thresholds and open-circuit for anomalous cross-tenant traffic; canary traffic is routed to isolated canary pools with telemetry sampled at 100% for 24h.

Threat model summary (top 3 realistic paths):
1) Misissued control-plane credentials -> Mitigation: Short-lived certs, automatic rotation, auditor alerts, HSM-backed signing, and immediate automated revocation propagation.
2) Sidecar compromise (escape to host) -> Mitigation: eBPF egress enforcement at host, mandatory seccomp, read-only rootfs, and node-level IDS; lateral movement flagged and node quarantined automatically.
3) Compromised third-party artifact (supply chain) -> Mitigation: Signed artifacts, SBOMs, immutable images scanned at deploy time, runtime attestation, and rollback playbooks.

Evidence pointers included in attachments: the PNG shows AZ mapping and peering, CSV contains recent allowlist deny/hit examples (sanitized). For the walkthrough we'll pull Live telemetry snippets and show correlation between request ID and audit log entry.

Ben Carter
Principal Infra Security Engineer
Redwood Inference
ben.carter@redwood.inference.com

A couple quick clarifications before the walkthrough: 1) can you confirm mean time-to-revoke for control-plane certs once an auditor triggers revocation? 2) For eBPF hooks — do you maintain deterministic ordering between sidecar egress rules and host-level policies so we can reason about fail-closed semantics? 3) Can you provide an example DocuSign or statement of attestation that your auditors would sign for tenant segregation (we'll need that in our submission).

We'll take the 09/23 10:00 PT slot — please send the calendar invite. Also: please attach the single-page attestation template if available (we can accept a draft).
